key_insight: The paper argues that VLA robots perform better when they learn an explicit prior over actions, instead of forcing the action head to discover motion patterns from scratch. This helps bridge the gap between strong visual-language understanding and reliable physical control across different robot bodies.
problem_solved: It addresses the lack of motion priors in standard Vision-Language-Action models, where the action module must simultaneously learn temporal dynamics, control, and cross-modal alignment. This becomes especially difficult for cross-embodiment manipulation, where robots have different bodies, kinematics, and action spaces.
method: Builds on a VLM backbone but adds a mechanism to learn reusable action priors for manipulation.
Separates motion knowledge from task-specific policy learning so the model can transfer better across robot embodiments.
Optimizes the policy with an explicit focus on action structure, reducing the burden on the action module to learn low-level dynamics from scratch.
impact: For practitioners, this suggests a more scalable path to robot manipulation models that transfer across platforms and require less embodiment-specific retraining. It can improve sample efficiency, stability, and generalization in real-world robotic systems.
